variants.title: Fit learned state safely
variants.context: Some transforms learn state from data: imputers learn replacement values, scalers learn distribution statistics, vocabularies learn categories, and selectors learn which inputs survive. The safe order is to create the evaluation boundary first, fit state on training evidence only, apply the frozen state to every other partition, then version preprocessing, feature definitions, and model artifact so they promote and roll back together.
variants.prompt: A churn model needs a median imputer and a standard scaler on six numeric columns. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Learn the medians and the scaling means and variances from the training partition only.
Version the preprocessing state, feature definitions, model artifact, and schema so they are promoted together.
Separate training and evaluation evidence by the correct entity and time unit before inspecting any statistics.
Apply that frozen state to validation, test, batch inference, and online inference inputs.

variants.hint: Which step decides what the held-out metric is allowed to claim?
variants.explanation: Split, fit, apply, version. Statistics learned from evaluation rows make the holdout score describe data the model already saw.

variants.title: Fit learned state safely

The safe order is to create the evaluation boundary first, fit state on training evidence only, apply the frozen state to every other partition, then version preprocessing, feature definitions, and model artifact so they promote and roll back together.
variants.prompt: A target encoder for a merchant column is evaluated with five-fold cross-validation. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Compute the encoding from that fold's training portion alone, not from the full table.
Transform the fold's held-out rows with the encoding fitted inside that fold.
Bind the final encoder, feature definition, and model into one versioned release.
Form the folds so each fold's training portion is separated from its held-out portion.

variants.hint: The rule applies once per fold, not once per experiment.
variants.explanation: Each fold must fit preprocessing and selection using only its own training portion, otherwise every fold's score borrows information from its holdout.

variants.title: Fit learned state safely
variants.context: Some transforms learn state from data: imputers learn replacement values, scalers learn distribution statistics, vocabularies learn categories, and selectors learn which inputs survive. The safe order is to create the evaluation boundary first, fit state on training evidence only, apply the frozen state to every other partition, then version preprocessing, feature definitions, and model artifact so they promote and roll back together.
variants.prompt: A vocabulary for a high-cardinality merchant identifier is being prepared for release. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Build the vocabulary from training rows and define what happens for an unknown category.
Draw the evaluation boundary so merchants seen only after the cutoff stay on the held-out side.
Promote the vocabulary artifact together with the model so a rollback returns both to the same state.
Apply the frozen vocabulary, including its unknown-category behavior, to every other partition and to serving.

variants.hint: Unknown categories are part of the frozen state, not an afterthought.
variants.explanation: A vocabulary is learned state. Fitting it on all rows leaks which categories will appear later, and shipping it separately from the model breaks rollback.

variants.title: Build a point-in-time row
variants.context: A historical training row asks what the system could have known for this entity at this prediction timestamp. Two clocks matter: event time is when the source event happened, and availability time is when it became usable by the feature pipeline. A correct join also enforces the entity key, the window boundary, and any time-to-live policy.
variants.prompt: A training row needs a 30-day purchase count for one customer as of a specific scoring moment. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Restrict the candidate events to the same customer entity key.
Drop events whose availability time is not earlier than the prediction timestamp.
Fix the prediction timestamp that this training row is being built for.
Apply the 30-day window and the time-to-live policy, then emit the value or its documented default.
Drop events whose event time is not earlier than the prediction timestamp.

variants.hint: Two clocks have to pass, not one.
variants.explanation: The row may only contain what the system could actually have read at that moment, so both event time and availability time are filtered.

variants.title: Build a point-in-time row
variants.context: A historical training row asks what the system could have known for this entity at this prediction timestamp. Two clocks matter: event time is when the source event happened, and availability time is when it became usable by the feature pipeline. A correct join also enforces the entity key, the window boundary, and any time-to-live policy.
variants.prompt: A purchase happened at 09:40 but a batch outage delayed it until 14:00, and a prediction was made at 11:00. Put the steps in order for the row built at 11:00.

items.text: Emit the window value computed without that purchase, matching what serving could have returned.
Fix the prediction timestamp at 11:00 for this entity.
Collect the entity's candidate purchase events, including the one stamped 09:40.
Keep the 09:40 event after the event-time filter, since it happened before the prediction.
Remove it at the availability-time filter, because the pipeline could not read it until 14:00.

variants.hint: Happening before the prediction is not the same as being readable before it.
variants.explanation: A record that arrived after the prediction would create training-serving skew if a later backfill let it into the historical row.

variants.title: Build a point-in-time row
variants.context: A historical training row asks what the system could have known for this entity at this prediction timestamp. Two clocks matter: event time is when the source event happened, and availability time is when it became usable by the feature pipeline. A correct join also enforces the entity key, the window boundary, and any time-to-live policy.
variants.prompt: The only eligible value for an entity is older than the feature's time-to-live. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Emit the declared null fallback instead of the expired value, and record that the default was used.
Fix the prediction timestamp for the entity being scored.
Select the entity's latest value that satisfies both the event-time and availability-time filters.
Compare that value's age against the feature's declared time-to-live.

variants.hint: Eligibility has an upper age as well as a lower bound.
variants.explanation: Time to live is part of the feature contract, and recording default use is what later lets a default-rate spike be detected.

variants.title: Check the four invariants
variants.context: A production feature must satisfy four invariants. Available means the value exists when the prediction is requested. Reproducible means the same entity, timestamp, inputs, and feature version give the same value offline and online. Useful means it improves a holdout metric or important slice enough to justify its cost. Operable means it has a type, owner, source, freshness target, null policy, lineage, monitoring plan, and safe fallback.
variants.prompt: Match each feature invariant to what it requires.

pairs.label: Available
pairs.detail: The value exists when the prediction is requested, with no future or late-arriving information.

pairs.label: Reproducible
pairs.detail: The same entity, timestamp, inputs, and version give the same value on the offline and online paths.

pairs.label: Useful
pairs.detail: The feature improves a holdout metric or an important slice enough to justify its complexity and cost.

pairs.label: Operable
pairs.detail: The feature has a type, owner, source, freshness target, null policy, lineage, monitoring, and fallback.

variants.hint: One invariant is about time, one about agreement, one about evidence, one about ownership.
variants.explanation: A feature has to satisfy all four. Predictive power alone says nothing about whether the value is deployable.

variants.prompt: A review finds four problems with proposed features. Match each problem to the invariant it violates.

pairs.label: A chargeback flag written 30 days after the decision appears in the training row
The batch job rounds a ratio to two decimals while the serving path does not
A new column moves the holdout metric by less than its measurement noise
Nobody can say what the feature should return when its source is down

variants.hint: Ask what each feature would do at the moment of a real prediction.
variants.explanation: Naming the violated invariant points at the fix: change the timing, unify the definition, drop the feature, or write the contract.

variants.title: Check the four invariants
variants.context: A production feature must satisfy four invariants. Available means the value exists when the prediction is requested. Reproducible means the same entity, timestamp, inputs, and feature version give the same value offline and online. Useful means it improves a holdout metric or important slice enough to justify its cost. Operable means it has a type, owner, source, freshness target, null policy, lineage, monitoring plan, and safe fallback.
variants.prompt: A second review finds four more problems. Match each problem to the invariant it violates.

pairs.label: A window is computed from a table that is only refreshed hours after prediction time
Two teams maintain separate implementations of the same aggregate
An expensive external enrichment matches an existing cheap feature on every slice
No monitor would notice if the feature silently returned its default for every entity

variants.hint: Duplicated implementations and missing monitors fail different invariants.
variants.explanation: Two independently maintained implementations of one feature break reproducibility, and an unmonitored default is an operability gap, not a modeling gap.

variants.title: Choose a selection method
variants.context: Filter methods rank inputs with statistics independent of the final model: cheap, but they miss interactions. Wrapper methods train repeated candidate subsets against the chosen metric: model-specific, but expensive and unstable on small data. Embedded methods use regularization, tree splits, or learned gates during fit, and their stability must be checked across folds and time periods.
variants.prompt: A team has 4,000 candidate columns and one afternoon to narrow them before any model training. What should they reach for first?
options: Embedded methods, fitting a regularized model on all 4,000 columns at once.
Filter methods, ranking inputs with model-independent statistics as a cheap first screen.
Wrapper methods, training candidate subsets so the ranking reflects the final model.
optionFeedback: This is a reasonable later step, but it still requires a full fit rather than the quick screen that was asked for.
Correct: filters are inexpensive at this width, provided the team remembers they can miss interactions.
Repeated subset training over 4,000 columns will not finish in an afternoon.
variants.hint: What is the budget, and what is the screen allowed to prove?
variants.explanation: Filter methods are a screen, not proof of production value. They cost little and they miss interactions.

variants.title: Choose a selection method
variants.context: Filter methods rank inputs with statistics independent of the final model: cheap, but they miss interactions. Wrapper methods train repeated candidate subsets against the chosen metric: model-specific, but expensive and unstable on small data. Embedded methods use regularization, tree splits, or learned gates during fit, and their stability must be checked across folds and time periods.
variants.prompt: A model with 25 candidate features shows strong interactions, compute is plentiful, and the team wants selection tied to the metric they actually optimize. Which method fits, and what must they watch?
options: Wrapper methods, watching for instability because subset search overfits small datasets.
Filter methods, watching for cost because ranking statistics scale poorly to 25 columns.
Embedded methods, watching for the fact that they cannot capture feature interactions.
optionFeedback: Correct: repeated subset experiments capture model-specific interactions, at the price of compute and stability risk.
Filters are the cheap option at any width, and they are the method least able to see the interactions described.
Tree splits and learned gates do capture interactions, so the stated caveat is wrong.
variants.hint: Which method actually trains the model it is selecting for?
variants.explanation: Wrapper methods capture model-specific interactions but can be unstable on small data, so stability across folds has to be checked.

variants.title: Choose a selection method
variants.context: Filter methods rank inputs with statistics independent of the final model: cheap, but they miss interactions. Wrapper methods train repeated candidate subsets against the chosen metric: model-specific, but expensive and unstable on small data. Embedded methods use regularization, tree splits, or learned gates during fit, and their stability must be checked across folds and time periods.
variants.prompt: A gradient-boosted model already prunes weak inputs during fit. The team wants to use that to reduce the feature set. What should they do before trusting it?
options: Accept the retained set, since selection during fit is measured against the training objective.
Validate that the retained set is stable across folds, seeds, and out-of-time windows.
Confirm that the importances rank the features in the same order as a filter statistic.
optionFeedback: The training objective is exactly the evidence that cannot confirm generalization to unseen data.
Correct: embedded selection is a model decision, and a set that changes per seed is not a reliable one.
Agreement with a model-independent statistic is not required and would defeat the point of an embedded method.
variants.hint: Would the same features survive if the seed changed?
variants.explanation: Embedded selection reduces effective inputs during fit, but its result must be validated for stability across folds and time periods.

variants.title: Diagnose the feature in production
variants.context: Monitor the mechanism, not only the distribution. Drift can be legitimate while a stable distribution hides a broken pipeline. Compare offline and online values for sampled entity and timestamp pairs, alert on late data, stale values, schema changes, and default-rate spikes, and track feature versions alongside predictions and outcomes.
variants.prompt: Online serving returns the declared null fallback for 20 percent of entities while the offline table has real values for them. The distribution monitor on the feature is green. What is the most likely reading?
options: The population genuinely changed, since a green distribution check means offline and online agree.
The offline table is stale, because a fallback is only returned when the source has no value at all.
The online path is failing and the distribution check cannot see it, so the default rate is the signal to alert on.
optionFeedback: A distribution check compares shapes within one path and never establishes that two paths agree.
Fallbacks are also returned when the online store is unreachable or the value is past its time to live.
Correct: defaults can hold a distribution steady while a fifth of predictions run on no real evidence.
variants.hint: Which monitor would notice a value that is merely missing?
variants.explanation: A stable distribution can hide a broken pipeline. Default rate and offline-online comparison catch what a shape check cannot.

variants.title: Diagnose the feature in production
variants.context: Monitor the mechanism, not only the distribution. Drift can be legitimate while a stable distribution hides a broken pipeline. Compare offline and online values for sampled entity and timestamp pairs, alert on late data, stale values, schema changes, and default-rate spikes, and track feature versions alongside predictions and outcomes.
variants.prompt: A backfill changed a window definition. Offline values for the last 90 days are now different, and the online materialization still uses the old rule. What should happen before the model is promoted?
options: Replay sampled entity and timestamp pairs through both paths and require them to match.
Retrain on the corrected offline values, since the offline path is the source of truth.
Wait for the online store to converge naturally as new events overwrite old values.
optionFeedback: Correct: parity replay is the release gate that catches a definition living in only one path.
Training on values serving cannot produce is the definition of training-serving skew.
The rule differs, not the data, so new events are computed with the old definition and never converge.
variants.hint: Which path will the model actually read at prediction time?
variants.explanation: One definition, two materializations. A changed definition must reach both paths and be proven equal by replay before promotion.

variants.title: Diagnose the feature in production
variants.context: Monitor the mechanism, not only the distribution. Drift can be legitimate while a stable distribution hides a broken pipeline. Compare offline and online values for sampled entity and timestamp pairs, alert on late data, stale values, schema changes, and default-rate spikes, and track feature versions alongside predictions and outcomes.
variants.prompt: A drift alert fires on a spend feature. Parity replay matches, the default rate is flat, the schema is unchanged, and freshness is inside target. What is the right conclusion?
options: The mechanism is healthy, so investigate the product change behind the shift before acting on it.
The feature is broken in a way the parity replay is too coarse to detect.
The alert is noise and the drift threshold should be widened to stop it firing.
optionFeedback: Correct: with the operational invariants holding, the shift is most likely real behavior that deserves product context.
Every mechanism check passed, so asserting a hidden break has no evidence behind it.
Widening the threshold removes the signal instead of explaining it, and the next real shift goes unseen.
variants.explanation: Pair statistical checks with operational invariants. When the invariants hold, a shift is a prompt to investigate the product, not proof of a defect.
